source.title: Learning Latent Protein Languages for Autoregressive Generation
source.authors: Mahdi Pourmirzaei; Farzaneh Esmaili; Amir Ziashahabi; Mohammadreza Pourmirzaei; Dong Xu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends compute-based loss scaling analysis to protein sequence and structure-token language models, a new modality relative to the cited text-language-model scaling work.
record.gate_note: The scaling results are validation cross-entropy versus estimated downstream autoregressive training compute, with fitted exponents reported in Section 4.2.1. The paper also reports generation, structure prediction, and a tokenizer comparison, but those results do not test the claim versions about scaling, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, or downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss. Figure 5 shows per-run curves, but does not provide their individual loss values numerically.
record.test_reason: The study fits validation cross-entropy against downstream training compute for autoregressive protein models: amino-acid, PLL and SLL token spaces, 17.9M–1.33B parameters, about 10^2–10^6 PFLOPs. It reports power-law exponents, which bear on whether the power-law form carries over to a non-text modality (V5). The amino-acid vs PLL exponent gap under matched training bears on setup-dependence of exponents (V7). These are protein-sequence and structure-token models, not text language models, so the results bear on V5 rather than V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that under matched downstream sequence training, PLLM has a roughly 1.9× steeper fitted compute-scaling exponent than the amino-acid model (0.038 vs 0.020). SLLM has α = 0.049, which they call numerically close to Kaplan's text exponent, though the comparison is qualitative. They do not treat absolute cross-entropy across vocabularies as comparable, and note that representation-building compute is excluded and total resources are not matched.
record.recipe_differences: Uses autoregressive next-token models and validation cross-entropy against compute with power-law fitting, but fits zero-offset laws to lower-loss frontiers and excludes tokenizer learning, encoder pretraining, and preprocessing from compute. The SLLM data and exposure differ from the matched amino-acid/PLLM comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported exponents vary across token representations; SLLM also uses different data and training exposure. The fit uses a zero-offset law, and the paper does not report sensitivity to alternative fitting choices.
record.problems: Only six completed runs per token space are selected for fitting. Fit confidence intervals and sensitivity to an additive irreducible-loss term are not reported. Compute estimates cover downstream autoregressive training only; representation-building resources are excluded, and the authors note that total resources are not matched. SLLM uses different data and training exposure from the amino-acid model and PLLM.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-fit outcomes were reported numerically. Figure 5 plots individual validation-loss points but does not give their exact values in text or tables; those values were not transcribed as separate rows.

untested.parts: No text language models; the protein results are treated under V5.
No extrapolation from small-run fits to larger runs.
No fixed-parameter shape comparison; depth and width co-vary along the grid.
Only protein sequence and structure-token autoregressive pretraining. No image, video, repeated-data-specific, fine-tuning or transfer scaling. Fit quality and an irreducible-loss term are untested.
Downstream generation metrics are not related to scale or loss.
No alternative fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules, or tests of curvature away from a single power law. Only the token-representation choice is varied.

missing.what: A length-conditioning continuation curriculum lowers SLLM unconditional validation loss from 3.891 to 3.670 (5.70%). The authors frame this as improving the loss-compute frontier. It is a single-model training-regime effect, not a scaling fit, so it is noted for completeness only.

record.verdict_notes: Only six runs per token space. The zero-offset OLS fit is on a lower-loss frontier of validation points across training steps; no irreducible-loss term, confidence intervals or goodness-of-fit are reported. A steeper exponent in a different vocabulary is not directly a quality comparison, since the loss scales differ. The amino-acid exponent of 0.020 is very shallow.

versions.untested_parts: Tests fitted validation-loss scaling against compute; does not independently vary parameters or training tokens, or establish that the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No test of predictions from small-run fits on much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for loss-minimising parameter and token allocations.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests protein sequence and structure-token models only; does not test image or video models, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No analysis of whether downstream-task performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.

The fitted exponent differs between amino-acid and PLL representations, but the study does not test alternative fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, or compute-optimal allocation; it reports no test for bending away from a single power law.

rows.note: The text reports this exponent for the amino-acid model. The shared architecture grid is listed in Table 10; Figure 5 labels this series with sizes from 15.8M to 605.5M, while the appendix grid lists 17.9M to 1.33B.
rows.check: Should not link to V1, which concerns text LM pretraining; protein tokens are a different modality (V5). The size discrepancy is likely not an error: Table 10 labels include the PLL/SLL 4,096-token embedding, and the amino-acid model's small vocabulary gives fewer parameters (Fig. 5a legend 15.8M–1.32B). Fit quality and confidence intervals are not reported.

rows.note: The authors state that SLLM has different training exposure from the amino-acid model and PLLM, and that absolute cross-entropy across vocabularies is not treated as a common quality scale.
rows.check: Remove V1. V7 link removed: SLLM differs from r1/r2 in data, epochs, token count and minimum learning rate, so its exponent gap is confounded and does not isolate a setup or fitting choice.

relationships.condition: Autoregressive protein models on amino-acid, PLL and SLL tokens, 17.9M–1.33B params, ~10^2–10^6 PFLOPs
relationships.reason: Validation loss vs compute is fit by a zero-offset power law in all three token spaces, with α = 0.020, 0.038 and 0.049 (r1–r3). Fit quality and confidence intervals are not reported, and the frontier is built from within-run validation points.
relationships.display_finding: Zero-offset compute power laws fitted validation loss with α values of 0.020, 0.038 and 0.049 for amino-acid, PLL and SLL tokens, respectively; the frontier used within-run validation points, without reported fit quality or confidence intervals.

relationships.condition: Amino-acid vs PLL tokenization under the same data, architecture grid, token budget and optimizer
relationships.reason: Changing only the target token representation nearly doubles the fitted exponent (0.020 vs 0.038; r1, r2). This shows the exponent depends on a setup choice, here tokenization.
relationships.display_finding: Changing only the target representation from amino-acid to PLL tokens increased the fitted exponent from 0.020 to 0.038.
